items.question: Read the sentence and choose the meaning of the word in capitals as it is used here. Her CANDID assessment of the project surprised the board: she listed the three failures plainly, praised the one success, and recommended stopping the work.
items.explanation: Listing failures plainly while also praising the one success is frank honesty, not flattery, evasion or hostility.

items.question: Read the sentence and choose the meaning of the word in capitals as it is used here. The BENIGN tumour could be removed with a simple operation, and the doctors told the family that it would not spread or return.
items.explanation: A tumour removed by a simple operation that will not spread or return is harmless, not malignant, painful or mysterious.

items.question: Read the sentence and choose the meaning of the word in capitals as it is used here. The FASTIDIOUS editor returned the manuscript with forty notes, objecting to a misplaced comma on page three and a repeated word on page forty.
items.explanation: Forty notes about a comma and a repeated word show excessive attention to small details, not carelessness, slowness or generosity.

items.question: Read the sentence and choose the meaning of the word in capitals as it is used here. The AUDACIOUS plan to build the plant in nine months, half the usual time, depended on three suppliers delivering on the same day and no rain for a month.
options: bold and willing to take risks
items.explanation: Building in half the usual time while depending on same-day deliveries and a month without rain is bold risk-taking, not caution, secrecy or waste.

items.question: Read the sentence and choose the meaning of the word in capitals as it is used here. The DOCILE crowd accepted the new rules without a single protest, queuing quietly and following every instruction the marshals gave.
items.explanation: Accepting rules without protest and following every instruction is obedience, not rebellion, confusion or anger.

items.question: Read the sentence and choose the meaning of the word in capitals as it is used here. The ERRATIC power supply, failing for an hour on Monday, returning on Tuesday and failing again on Wednesday, made it impossible to run the machines on schedule.
items.explanation: Failing, returning and failing again on successive days is irregular, not steady, constant or wasteful.

items.question: Read the sentence and choose the meaning of the word in capitals as it is used here. The report was praised for its CANDOUR: it admitted the project's failures plainly, named the managers responsible, and did not soften the findings to protect anyone.
items.explanation: Candour means frankness and honesty. The sentence shows it in action: admitting failures plainly, naming those responsible and refusing to soften the findings. Carefulness and precision describe how the report is written, not the openness the sentence emphasises.

items.question: Read the four sentences and choose the one that is grammatically correct.

The number of applicants have risen sharply, and each of them has been asked to submit an extra document.
The number of applicants has risen sharply, and each of them have been asked to submit an extra document.

items.question: Read the four sentences and choose the one that is grammatically correct.
options: Neither the students nor the teacher are satisfied with the timetable, and the principal has promised a revision.
Neither the students nor the teacher is satisfied with the timetable, and the principal have promised a revision.
Neither the students nor the teacher is satisfied with the timetable, and the principal has promised a revision.
Neither the students nor the teacher are satisfied with the timetable, and the principal have promised a revision.

items.passage:
When a large company advertises a job today, the first reader of the applications is usually not a person. It is software that scans resumes for keywords, ranks candidates, and rejects most of them before any human looks at the pile. The software is sold as a solution to a real problem: a popular vacancy can attract thousands of applications, and no hiring team can read them all carefully. Automation promises speed, consistency and freedom from the whims of individual recruiters. That promise is attractive, and it is also, in important ways, false.
The problem begins with the data the software learns from. A hiring model trained on a company's past hiring decisions will learn the patterns in those decisions, including the biases. If the company historically hired mostly men for technical roles, the model will learn to prefer resumes that resemble those of the men it hired, downranking resumes that use the language of women's colleges or of career breaks taken for childcare. When the bias is discovered, the usual fix is to remove the obvious markers, such as gender and college names. But the model then finds proxies: the sports played, the clubs joined, the wording of a hobby. Bias removed from one variable reappears in another, because the history it learned from is itself biased.
A second problem is what the software rewards. Keyword matching favours candidates who know how to write for the machine, using the exact phrases from the job description, over candidates whose experience is real but described differently. A nurse who ran a ward and a manager who ran a team may have the same skill, but only one of them will have used the word the software is looking for. The result is a filter that selects for fluency in a particular dialect of corporate language, which correlates with privilege far more than with ability. Candidates from smaller towns, from non-English backgrounds, or from jobs that never needed such language are filtered out before their competence is ever assessed. The system is consistent, which is the vendors' claim, but it is consistently wrong in the same direction.
Defenders of automated hiring reply that human recruiters are worse. A human can be tired, prejudiced, or simply careless, and two humans will disagree about the same resume. That is true, and it is the strongest argument for automation. But it confuses two different claims: that machines are more consistent than humans, and that machines are fair. Consistency is a property of the process; fairness is a property of the outcome. A machine that rejects the same kind of candidate every time is perfectly consistent and perfectly unfair. The question is not whether the machine is consistent, but whether the pattern it applies is one we would endorse if we could see it plainly.
The practical answer is neither to ban the software nor to trust it blindly. Companies should be required to test their hiring tools for disparate outcomes, to publish the results, and to keep a human in the loop for every rejection that the software proposes. Candidates should be told when a machine has assessed them and given a way to challenge the assessment. And hiring teams should remember what the software cannot do: it cannot judge potential, it cannot recognise a career that does not fit the usual shape, and it cannot take responsibility for a decision. Those remain human tasks, and a hiring process that forgets them will keep making the same efficient, consistent, and unjust decisions at ever greater speed.
items.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the things the passage says hiring software cannot do?
options: Recognise a career that does not fit the usual shape
items.explanation: The passage says the software cannot judge potential, cannot recognise an unusual career shape and cannot take responsibility for a decision. Reading thousands of applications quickly is exactly what it can do, so it is not one of the things it cannot do.

items.question: Which of the following statements are true according to the passage? (A) A hiring model trained on a company's past decisions will reproduce the company's historical biases even if no one programs it to discriminate. (B) Keyword matching can reject a competent candidate whose experience is described in different words. (C) The passage claims human recruiters are fairer than software.
items.explanation: A is true: a model trained on past hiring learns the patterns in those decisions, including the biases, and bias removed from one variable reappears in another. B is true: a nurse who ran a ward and a manager who ran a team may have the same skill, but only one will have used the word the software is looking for. C is false: the passage says humans can be tired, prejudiced or careless, and that consistency is not fairness.

items.question: In the passage, the word 'proxies' is used to mean
options: variables the model uses instead of gender because they predict job performance better
deliberate attempts by candidates to hide their background
official categories the company uses to sort applicants
other variables that stand in for a removed marker and carry the same bias
items.explanation: When gender and college names are removed, the model finds proxies such as the sports played and the clubs joined, which carry the same bias. They are not better predictors of performance, not candidates' attempts to hide, and not official categories.

items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the passage's claim that keyword matching filters out competent candidates unfairly?
options: Candidates from small towns often lack corporate vocabulary.
In a controlled test, identical experience described in plain language was ranked far below the same experience described with the job description's exact phrases.
Most large companies now use hiring software.
Some hiring managers admit they are sometimes tired.
items.explanation: The claim is that the filter rewards wording rather than competence. A controlled test showing identical experience ranked differently purely because of phrasing proves the mechanism directly. The other options are background facts that do not test the mechanism.

items.question: The author's main conclusion about hiring software is that
options: hiring software should be tested for unfair outcomes, kept under human oversight, and never allowed to replace human judgement of potential.
hiring software is already fair because it is consistent.
human recruiters are fairer than any software.
hiring software should be banned in all large companies.
items.explanation: The author rejects both banning the software and trusting it blindly, and calls for outcome testing, published results, human review of rejections and candidate challenge rights. The other options state positions the author explicitly rejects.

items.passage:
A small manufacturer in Coimbatore who wants to buy a second machine faces a problem that has little to do with the machine. The machine costs forty lakh rupees, the order book justifies it, and the bank, in principle, is willing to lend. The difficulty is proof. The bank wants three years of audited statements, collateral worth more than the loan, and a credit history that a firm of twelve employees rarely has. The manufacturer has instead a decade of steady orders, a reputation with buyers, and a bank account that shows money coming in every month. None of that counts as proof in the form the bank requires. The result is a familiar paradox: the firms that most need credit are the ones least able to document that they deserve it, and the firms that can document it often need it least.
The gap is not small. India's micro, small and medium enterprises employ crores of people and supply large firms with parts, yet a large share of their credit demand is met by informal lenders at rates that would alarm any regulator. The informal lender asks no questions about audited statements; he knows the borrower, visits the workshop, and charges for the risk he takes. The formal system, by contrast, is cheap but blind: it lends at low rates to those it can see clearly, and cannot see the small manufacturer at all. The policy problem is therefore not a shortage of money, but a shortage of sight. The money exists; the information that would let it flow to the right borrower does not.
Technology has begun to change what a bank can see. A firm's GST filings show its sales month by month. Its electricity bills show whether the machines are running. Its payments through digital rails show who its customers are and whether they pay on time. Put together, these trails form a picture of a business that is in some ways more reliable than an audited statement, because it is harder to fabricate a year's worth of GST filings than a single document. The early results are encouraging: default rates on such loans have been low, which suggests that the information is genuinely informative, not merely novel.
There are, however, three cautions. The first is privacy: the same trails that let a lender see a business also let it see a great deal about the owner's life, and the consent for that seeing is often buried in a form the borrower does not read. The second is concentration: if only a few large platforms hold the data, they become gatekeepers who can decide which firms get credit and on what terms. The third is that data cannot replace judgement entirely. A GST trail shows sales, but it does not show whether the owner is honest, whether the order book will last, or whether a single large customer might disappear. A lender that trusts the trail completely will eventually be surprised by the borrower the trail could not describe.
The sensible conclusion is that data should widen the bank's sight, not replace it. Let the trails qualify a borrower for a first, small loan, and let the repayment of that loan build the formal credit history that the bank wanted in the first place. Regulate who may use the trails and for what, so that consent means something and gatekeepers cannot exploit their position. And keep a human in the decision for larger loans, where judgement matters most.
items.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the three cautions the passage raises about data-based lending?
options: High default rates on data-based loans
Privacy: the trails reveal a great deal about the owner's life
Concentration: a few large platforms could become gatekeepers
items.explanation: The passage raises privacy, concentration and the limits of data as its three cautions. It says default rates on data-based loans have been low, so high default rates are not one of the cautions.

items.question: Which of the following statements are true according to the passage? (A) The passage implies that informal lending persists because the formal system cannot see small borrowers, not because money is scarce. (B) GST filings are harder to fabricate than a single audited statement. (C) The author recommends that data trails replace human judgement for all loans.
items.explanation: A is true: the policy problem is not a shortage of money but a shortage of sight. B is true: it is harder to fabricate a year's worth of GST filings than a single document. C is false: the author says to keep a human in the decision for larger loans, where judgement matters most.

items.question: In the passage, the phrase 'a shortage of sight' means that
options: the formal credit system lacks the information needed to judge small borrowers
the small firm has no financial records of any kind
banks have too little money to lend
regulators cannot see the informal lending market at all
items.explanation: The passage says the money exists but the information that would let it flow to the right borrower does not. The firm does have records in GST filings, bills and payment trails, just not in the form the bank requires; the problem is the lender's sight, not the money supply or regulators.

items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the passage's claim that data trails make lending to small firms safer?
options: Most small firms file GST returns through agents who routinely inflate sales figures to obtain larger loans.
Informal lenders charge very high interest rates.
A few large platforms hold most of the transaction data.
Some borrowers do not read consent forms carefully.
items.explanation: The claim rests on trails being harder to fabricate than a single document. If agents routinely inflate GST sales figures, the trail itself is unreliable, which attacks the mechanism directly. The other options are cautions the passage already raises or background facts.

items.question: The author's main recommendation for small-firm credit is that
options: banks should stop asking small firms for any documents.
informal lenders should be banned immediately.
data trails should qualify borrowers for a first small loan that builds a formal credit history, with regulation of data use and human judgement for larger loans.
small firms should be given loans with no credit checks at all.
items.explanation: The author concludes that trails should widen the bank's sight, qualify a borrower for a first small loan, build credit history through repayment, regulate data use, and keep humans in larger decisions. The other options state extremes the author rejects.

items.question: Choose the pair of idioms that fits the two sentences. (1) The report ___ the problem, praising the plan while ignoring its cost. (2) The committee ___ the decision until the survey results arrived.
items.explanation: Glossed over means to treat a problem lightly and pass over its difficulties, which fits a report that praises the plan while ignoring its cost. Put off means to postpone, which fits a committee delaying a decision until survey results arrive. Called off means cancelled, which fits neither the report nor a delayed decision. Brought up means raised for discussion, which is the opposite of ignoring the cost. Set aside means to reserve or dismiss, which does not fit the report's treatment of the problem.

items.question: Choose the idiom that fits both sentences. (1) The two departments decided to ___ on the project, sharing staff and budgets. (2) The rival firms decided to ___ on the research, pooling their laboratories.
items.explanation: Both sentences describe rivals cooperating and pooling resources. 'Part ways' and 'go it alone' are the opposite, and 'cut corners' is about doing things cheaply, not cooperating.

items.question: Choose the idiom that fits both sentences. (1) The manager's excuse did not ___ with the committee, which asked for the documents instead. (2) His story did not ___ with the police, who found the dates did not match.
items.explanation: Both sentences describe an explanation that does not stand up to scrutiny. The other idioms describe easing tension, failing or evading a question, none of which fits either sentence.

items.question: A statement that is so obvious it needs no proof and is accepted as a starting point for reasoning is called?
items.explanation: An axiom is accepted without proof as a starting point. A theorem needs proof, a hypothesis needs testing, and a paradox only seems contradictory.

items.question: A substance that both neutralises a poison and is given as the specific treatment for it is called?
items.explanation: An antidote both neutralises a poison and is its specific treatment. A vaccine prevents disease, an antibiotic kills bacteria, and a sedative only calms.

items.question: A person who both lives at the same time as another and belongs to the same period is called?
items.explanation: A contemporary lives at the same time as another person and belongs to the same period. A successor and a descendant come after, and a predecessor comes before.

items.question: Arrange the following sentences in a logical order. A. Their teacher began reading one story aloud every Friday, and the children started to ask for the books she read from. B. A village school had no library, and its children had never read a book outside their textbooks. C. Within a year, the cupboard had grown into a small library run by the children themselves. D. At first the children borrowed only picture books, afraid the rest would be too hard. E. A retired teacher donated two hundred books and a cupboard to keep them in. Choose the correct order.
items.explanation: The correct order is BEDAC: A village school had no library, and... / A retired teacher donated two hundred books... / At first the children borrowed only picture... / Their teacher began reading one story aloud... / Within a year, the cupboard had grown... Every other option places a consequence before its cause or a reply before the statement it answers, breaking one of these links.

items.question: Arrange the following sentences in a logical order. A. Passengers booked in large numbers, but many were first-time flyers who needed extra help at the airport. B. It learned that a low fare brings a different customer, and the service must be designed for that customer. C. The airline offered very cheap tickets on a new route to fill its planes quickly. D. The airline responded by adding ground staff and charging for extra baggage, which annoyed the very passengers it had attracted. E. Queues grew, flights were delayed, and the airline's costs rose instead of falling. Choose the correct order.
items.explanation: The correct order is CAEDB: The airline offered very cheap tickets on... / Passengers booked in large numbers, but many... / Queues grew, flights were delayed, and the... / The airline responded by adding ground staff... / It learned that a low fare brings... Every other option places a consequence before its cause or a reply before the statement it answers, breaking one of these links.

items.question: Arrange the following sentences in a logical order. A. Five years later, the shaded stretches were measurably cooler than the bare ones. B. In the first summer, half the saplings died because nobody had been assigned to water them. C. The municipality, seeing the response, began paying the groups a small maintenance grant. D. The city decided to plant a lakh of trees along its roads to cut dust and heat. E. Residents' groups then adopted stretches of road and took turns watering the surviving trees. Choose the correct order.
items.explanation: The correct order is DBECA: The city decided to plant a lakh... / In the first summer, half the saplings... / Residents' groups then adopted stretches of road... / The municipality, seeing the response, began paying... / Five years later, the shaded stretches were... Every other option places a consequence before its cause or a reply before the statement it answers, breaking one of these links.

items.question: Two articles both cost Rs 400. Article A is first increased by 10% and then decreased by 30%. Article B is first decreased by 30% and then increased by 10%. By how much does the dearer article exceed the cheaper one?
items.explanation: Article A ends at Rs 400 x 1.1 x 0.7 = Rs 308, and article B ends at Rs 400 x 0.7 x 1.1 = Rs 308. Multiplication does not depend on the order, so both end at the same price and neither exceeds the other by anything. The other options come from applying only part of the two changes, which is not the difference between the two articles.

items.question: A number is first increased by 25% and then decreased by 10%, and the result is 900. What was the original number?
items.explanation: Working backwards, before the decrease the number was 900 x 100/90 = 1000, and before the increase it was that value x 100/125 = 800. The other options stop after one step or treat the final value as the original, which ignores one of the two changes.

items.question: An article costs Rs 600. It is marked up by 50%, then sold at a discount of 25% on the marked price, and then 8% tax is charged on the selling price. How much does the customer finally pay?
items.explanation: The marked price is Rs 900. After the 25% discount the selling price is Rs 675. Tax of 8% on that is Rs 54, so the customer pays Rs 729. The other options stop at the marked price or the pre-tax price, which misses one of the three stages.

items.question: Class A has 20 students with average score 24 (scores range from 20 to 28). Class B has 30 students with average score 36 (scores range from 33 to 39). If 5 students are transferred from class B to class A, what is the maximum possible average score of class A after the transfer?
items.explanation: To maximise the new average, transfer the highest-scoring students from B, each scoring 39. The new total is 20 x 24 + 5 x 39 = 675 over 25 students, giving 27. Transferring average or lowest scorers gives a lower average, and the old average ignores the transfer entirely, so those options are wrong.

items.question: What is the difference between the compound interest and the simple interest on Rs 8000 at 15% per annum in the first year and 10% per annum in the second year?
items.explanation: The compound interest is Rs 8000 x 1.15 x 1.1 - Rs 8000 = Rs 2120, and the simple interest is Rs 8000 x 25% = Rs 2000. The difference is Rs 2120 - Rs 2000 = Rs 120. The usual two-year formula does not apply because the rate changes, so each year must be worked out separately.

items.question: A pump can both fill and empty a tank of 1200 cubic metres. Its emptying rate is 20 cubic metres per minute higher than its filling rate, and it needs 10 minutes less to empty the tank than to fill it. What is the filling rate of the pump, in cubic metres per minute?
items.explanation: Let the filling rate be x. Then 1200/x - 1200/(x + 20) = 10, which simplifies to x squared + 20x - 2400 = 0, giving x = 40 (the negative root is rejected). The emptying rate 60 is the most tempting wrong answer, and dividing the volume by the time difference ignores the rate difference entirely.

items.question: Two numbers are in the ratio 4:3. If 6 is added to each number, the ratio becomes 5:4. What is the first number?
items.explanation: Let the numbers be 4k and 3k. Then (4k + 6)/(3k + 6) = 5/4, which gives k = 6, so the numbers are 24 and 18. The first number is 24. The other options add 6 to a number without solving for k, which confuses the changed value with the original.

items.question: The average of 10 numbers is 70. One of the numbers, 50, is replaced by 90, and then another number, 60, is replaced by 80. What is the new average?
items.explanation: The total rises by 90 - 50 = 40 at the first replacement and by 80 - 60 = 20 at the second, so it rises by 60 in all. The average rises by 60/10 = 6, giving 70 + 6 = 76. Stopping after one replacement or adding the whole rise to the average both miss a step.

items.question: A, B and C can alone complete a work in 8, 12 and 24 days respectively. They work together for 2 days, after which A leaves. In how many more days will B and C together finish the remaining work?
items.explanation: Take the total work as 24 units. A, B and C do 3, 2 and 1 units a day, so in 2 days they complete 12 units, leaving 12. B and C together do 3 units a day, so they need 12/3 = 4 more days. The other options divide the remaining work by the wrong combined rate or ignore that A has left.

items.question: A car travels 200 km at 50 km/h, then halts for 2 hours, then travels 200 km at 100 km/h, then travels 100 km at 50 km/h. What is the average speed of the car excluding halts, and what is it including halts? Give the two speeds in order, in km/h.
items.explanation: The driving times are 200/50 = 4 hours, 200/100 = 2 hours and 100/50 = 2 hours, a total of 8 hours for 500 km, so the average speed excluding halts is 500/8 = 62.5 km/h. Including the 2-hour halt, the total time is 10 hours, so the average speed is 500/10 = 50 km/h.

items.question: A train crosses a platform 400 m long in 30 seconds and a platform 650 m long in 40 seconds. What is the length of the train, in metres?
items.explanation: The train covers 250 m more in 10 seconds, so its speed is 250/10 = 25 m/s, which is 90 km/h. In 30 seconds it covers 25 x 30 = 750 m, which is the train plus the first platform, so the train is 750 - 400 = 350 m long. A single platform and time cannot fix the length, because the speed is unknown.

items.question: 20 litres of a solution with 40% acid is mixed with 30 litres of a solution with 60% acid. How many litres of pure acid must be added to make the acid concentration of the resulting mixture 60%?
items.explanation: The mixture has 26 litres of acid in 50 litres. Adding 10 litres of pure acid gives 26 + 10 = 36 litres of acid in 50 + 10 = 60 litres, which is 60%. Simply adding the shortfall of 4 litres ignores that the added acid also increases the total volume.

items.question: The marked price of an article is Rs 1200. A shop offers two successive discounts of 15% and 10%, while another shop offers a single discount of 20%. By how much is the cheaper of the two offers cheaper than the other?
items.explanation: The successive discounts give Rs 918 and the single discount gives Rs 960, so the successive discounts is cheaper by Rs 42. The other options give one of the selling prices or only the first discount, which does not compare the two offers.

items.question: What is the smallest number greater than 150 which, when divided by 9 and by 12, leaves a remainder of 7 in each case?
items.explanation: A number leaving remainder 7 on division by both 9 and 12 is 7 more than a multiple of their LCM, 36. The multiples of 36 near 150 are 108 and 144, and 144 + 7 = 151 is the first value above 150. The other options are the previous or next such number, or simply 150 + 7, which is not a multiple of 36 plus 7.

items.question: In a factory, machine A produces 25% with 8% defective, machine B produces 50% with 4% defective, machine C produces 25% with 4% defective. A toy drawn at random is found to be defective. What is the probability that it was made on machine B? Give your answer as a fraction.
items.explanation: The total defective probability is the weighted sum 1/20, and machine B contributes 1/50 of it, so the required probability is 1/50/1/20 = 2/5. The machine's share of output and its defect rate are both tempting wrong answers, because each ignores the other factor and the base rate.

items.question: What is the smallest number which, when divided by 4, leaves a remainder of 1 and when divided by 9, leaves a remainder of 7?
items.explanation: Numbers leaving remainder 1 on division by 4 are 1, 5, 9, and so on. The first of them that also leaves remainder 7 on division by 9 is 25: 25 = 4 x 6 + 1 and 25 = 9 x 2 + 7. Adding the LCM to the remainder, or using the LCM alone, gives a number with the wrong remainders.

items.question: Let n be the smallest positive integer greater than 30 that is divisible by 5 and leaves a remainder of 2 when divided by 6. What is the unit digit of 3 raised to the power n plus 7 raised to the power n?
items.explanation: First find n. The multiples of 5 above 30 are 35, 40, 45, 50, and so on. Their remainders on division by 6 are 5, 4, 3 and 2, so n = 50. The unit digits of powers of 3 cycle 3, 9, 7, 1 and of 7 cycle 7, 9, 3, 1, with period 4. Since 50 leaves remainder 2 on division by 4, both 3^50 and 7^50 end in 9, so their sum ends in 8. An exponent leaving remainder 0 on division by 4 would give 2, and remainder 1 or 3 would give 0.

items.question: A quadratic equation x squared + bx + 56 = 0 has two positive roots. The sum of the squares of the roots is 113. What is the larger root?
items.explanation: Let the roots be a and b. Then ab = 56 and a squared + b squared = 113, so (a + b) squared = 113 + 2 x 56 = 225, giving a + b = 15, since both roots are positive. So a and b are the roots of t squared - 15t + 56 = 0, which factors as (t - 8)(t - 7) = 0. The roots are 8 and 7, so the larger root is 8. 15 is the sum of the roots, 7 is the smaller root, and 56 is their product.

items.question: A is 2 times as old as B. In 10 years, A will be 1.5 times as old as B. What is A's present age, in years?
items.explanation: Let B's present age be x. Then A is 2x, and in 10 years 2x + 10 = 1.5(x + 10), which gives x = 10, so A is 2 x 10 = 20 years old. The other options give B's age, A's age in 10 years, or the sum of the two ages.

items.question: The equation x squared - 18x + k = 0 has two roots, one of which is twice the other. What is the value of k?
items.explanation: Let the roots be y and 2y. Their sum is 3y = 18, so y = 6 and the roots are 6 and 12. Their product is k = 6 x 12 = 72. The other options confuse the product with the square of one root or with the sum of the roots.

items.question: The sum of two numbers is 10 and their product is 21. What is the sum of the cubes of the two numbers?
items.explanation: Let the numbers be x and y. Then x cubed + y cubed = (x + y) cubed - 3xy(x + y) = 10 cubed - 3 x 21 x 10 = 1000 - 630 = 370. Using the sum of squares formula, or only one of the two terms, gives the wrong options.

items.question: The ratio of the present ages of A and B is 7:5. After 6 years, the ratio of their ages will become 5:4. What is A's present age?
items.explanation: Let the ages be 7k and 5k. Then (7k + 6)/(5k + 6) = 5/4, which gives k = 2, so A is 7 x 2 = 14 years old. The other options give B's age, A's age after 6 years, or a value obtained by adding 6 to the ratio instead of to the ages.

items.question: The sum of the ages of A and B is 52 years, the sum of the ages of B and C is 38 years, and the sum of the ages of A and C is 46 years. What is B's age?
items.explanation: Adding all three sums gives twice the sum of the three ages, so A + B + C = 68. Subtracting the sum of A and C, 46, gives B = 68 - 46 = 22 years. The other options give A's age, C's age, or the total of the three ages.

items.question: A rectangle has perimeter 36 m and its length is 4 m more than its breadth. What is the area of the rectangle, in square metres?
items.explanation: Length plus breadth is 36/2 = 18 m, and length minus breadth is 4 m, so the length is 11 m and the breadth is 7 m. The area is 11 x 7 = 77 square metres. The other options square the length, multiply the perimeter by the breadth, or add an arbitrary amount.

items.question: A circle is inscribed in a square. If the radius of the circle is increased by 25%, by what percentage does the area of the region inside the square but outside the circle increase?
items.explanation: With radius r, the square has area 4r squared and the circle has area pi r squared, so the region between them has area (4 - pi) r squared. Increasing r by 25% multiplies every area by (1 + 25/100) squared = 1.56, so the region also grows by 56.25%. The region scales with the square of the radius, just as the circle does, so doubling the percentage or using the percentage once both miss the square.

items.question: A cuboid has length 3 cm, volume 90 cubic cm and total surface area 126 square cm. What is the larger of its other two dimensions, in cm?
items.explanation: The product of the other two dimensions is 90/3 = 30, and from the surface area their sum is 11. Two numbers with sum 11 and product 30 are 5 and 6, so the larger is 6 cm. The other options give the smaller dimension, the sum, or the product.

items.question: A five-digit number is formed using each of the digits 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 exactly once. How many such five-digit numbers are divisible by 4?
items.explanation: Divisibility by 4 depends on the last two digits. The possible endings are 04, 12, 20, 24, 32 and 40. For the three endings containing zero (04, 20, 40), the remaining three digits are all non-zero, giving 3! = 6 arrangements each, or 18 in all. For the three endings without zero (12, 24, 32), the remaining digits include zero, which cannot lead, giving 3! - 2! = 4 arrangements each, or 12 in all. The total is 18 + 12 = 30. Counting 6 arrangements for every ending ignores that zero cannot lead, and counting only the zero endings misses the other case.

items.question: A bag has 8 red balls and 4 blue balls. Two balls are drawn at random, one after another, without replacement. Given that at least one ball is red, what is the probability that both balls are red? Give your answer as a fraction.
items.explanation: The condition changes the sample space: pairs with at least one red number C(12,2) - C(4,2) = 66 - 6 = 60. Both red pairs number C(8,2) = 28, so the probability is 28/60 = 7/15. Using the unconditional sample space, or the probability of one red draw, both ignore the condition.

items.question: Two fair dice are thrown together. Given that at least one die shows an even number, what is the probability that the sum of the numbers shown is 5? Give your answer as a fraction.
items.explanation: The condition leaves 27 equally likely outcomes, those with at least one even number. Of these, 4 add to 5, so the probability is 4/27 = 4/27. Using all 36 outcomes ignores the condition, and counting only the pairs that add to 5 without checking the condition overcounts.

items.question: In a group of 300 students, 100 do only WhatsApp, 80 do only Instagram, 50 do only Telegram, 30 do exactly two of the three activities, and 10 do all three. 30 students do none of the three activities. How many students do at least one of the three activities, and how many do exactly one of the three? Give the at-least-one count first.
items.explanation: The numbers add up: 100 + 80 + 50 + 30 + 10 + 30 = 300. At least one activity is everyone except the 30 who do none, which is 270. Exactly one activity is 100 + 80 + 50 = 230.

items.question: Using the Sales table, if the year in which A was lowest is removed from the table, what is the ratio of A's total to C's total over the remaining years?

diagram.caption: Sales (in Rs lakh) of four products, 2021 to 2024

items.explanation: A was lowest in 2021, at 80, so 2021 is removed. Over 2022 to 2024, A totals 90 + 110 + 120 = 320 and C totals 50 + 50 + 40 = 140, and 320 : 140 simplifies to 16 : 7. Using the full four years gives 400 : 200, or 2 : 1, which is the trap for solvers who skip the removal step.

items.question: In the Sales table, for B, in which year was the year-on-year growth rate the highest?
items.explanation: The growth rates for B are 50/3% in 2022, 100/7% in 2023, 25/2% in 2024. The highest is in 2022. Comparing raw values instead of rates would pick a later year, which is the trap this question sets.

items.question: In the Sales table, in which year was A's share of that year's total across all columns the highest?
items.explanation: A's shares are 100/3% in 2021, 1800/47% in 2022, 2200/53% in 2023, 600/13% in 2024. The highest share is in 2024. The raw value of A rises every year, so a reader who compares raw values instead of shares picks the wrong year.

items.question: Which column of the Sales table fell by the largest percentage between 2021 and 2024?
items.explanation: The percentage changes from 2021 to 2024 are A: 50%, B: 50%, C: -100/3%, D: -75%. The largest fall is D at 75%. A column with a large absolute fall can have a small percentage fall, so the raw difference is not the answer.

items.question: In the Sales table, which of the following statements must be true?
options: The total of D exceeds the total of A.
A exceeded B in every year.
C in 2024 is less than half its 2021 value.
items.explanation: A exceeded B in every year: 80 over 60, 90 over 70, 110 over 80 and 120 over 90, so the third statement is true. C did not fall every year: it was 50 in both 2022 and 2023. The total of D is 100 while the total of A is 400, so D does not exceed A. C in 2024 is 40, while half its 2021 value of 60 is 30, so 40 is not less than half.

items.question: Using the bar chart of Number of students in five streams, in which stream did the number of students grow by the largest percentage between 2023 and 2024?
items.explanation: Percentage growth is Science 30/150 = 20%, Commerce 60/240 = 25%, Arts 40/200 = 20%, Law 30/120 = 25% and Medicine 40/90 = 44.4%. Medicine has the largest percentage growth, even though Commerce had the largest absolute increase.

items.question: In the bar chart of Number of students in five streams, if the category with the smallest 2023 value is excluded, by how much did the total rise from 2023 to 2024 across the remaining categories?
items.explanation: The smallest 2023 value is Medicine, at 90, so Medicine is excluded. The 2023 total across the remaining streams is 800 minus 90 = 710, and the 2024 total across them is 1,000 minus 130 = 870, so the rise is 870 minus 710 = 160. The full rise of 200 ignores the exclusion, 140 is the rise if the largest category is excluded instead, and 40 is Medicine's own rise.

items.question: In the bar chart of Number of students in five streams, in which category is the absolute difference between the 2024 value and the 2023 value the largest?
items.explanation: The differences are Science: 30, Commerce: 60, Arts: 40, Law: 30, Medicine: 40. The largest is Commerce with 60. The category with the highest percentage growth is not necessarily the one with the largest absolute difference, since the bases differ.

items.question: In the bar chart of Number of students in five streams, the 2024 value for Science is smudged and cannot be read. The average of the three largest 2024 values across the five categories is 240. What is the 2024 value for Science?
items.explanation: The readable 2024 values are Commerce 300, Arts 240, Law 150 and Medicine 130. Let Science's value be c. The three largest values must average 240, so they sum to 720. If c were below 180, the three largest would be 300, 240 and 150, averaging 230, which contradicts 240. If c were 180 or more, the three largest would be 300, 240 and c, so c = 720 - 300 - 240 = 180, which is consistent. So Science's 2024 value is 180. 240 is the stated average, not the missing value, and 150 is the next readable value.

items.question: In the bar chart of Number of students in five streams, which category grew by the highest percentage from 2023 to 2024?
items.explanation: The growth rates are Science: 20%, Commerce: 25%, Arts: 20%, Law: 25%, Medicine: 400/9%. The highest is Medicine. The largest absolute increase belongs to a different category, which is why the percentage, not the raw increase, decides this question.

items.passage: The two pie charts show how monthly budget allocation was divided in 2023 and 2024. In 2023 the shares were Study 40%, Sleep 30%, Sports 10%, Entertainment 12%, Others 8%, on a total of Rs 40000. The 2024 shares are shown in the pie chart, on a total of Rs 60000.
items.question: The 2023 shares were Study 40%, Sleep 30%, Sports 10%, Entertainment 12%, Others 8%, on a total of Rs 40,000. The 2024 shares are shown in the pie chart, on a total of Rs 60,000. In the Monthly budget allocation pie charts, by how much did the amount spent on Study change from 2023 to 2024?
items.explanation: The amount on Study in 2023 was 40% of Rs 40000, which is Rs 16000, and in 2024 it was 35% of Rs 60000, which is Rs 21000. The change is Rs 21000 - Rs 16000 = Rs 5000, an increase. The change must be worked out from each year's own share and total; working from one year's total alone, or from the shares alone, gives the wrong change.

items.question: The 2023 shares were Study 40%, Sleep 30%, Sports 10%, Entertainment 12%, Others 8%, on a total of Rs 40,000. The 2024 shares are shown in the pie chart, on a total of Rs 60,000. In the Monthly budget allocation pie charts, comparing the 2023 and 2024 shares, which category's share rose by the most percentage points?
items.explanation: The changes in percentage points are Study: -5, Sleep: +0, Sports: +5, Entertainment: -4, Others: +4. The largest rise is Sports. A category whose amount rose may still have lost share, so the share change, not the amount change, decides this question.

items.question: The 2023 shares were Study 40%, Sleep 30%, Sports 10%, Entertainment 12%, Others 8%, on a total of Rs 40,000. The 2024 shares are shown in the pie chart, on a total of Rs 60,000. In the Monthly budget allocation pie charts, by how much did the combined amount spent on Sleep and Sports increase from 2023 to 2024?
items.explanation: In 2023 the two categories together were 40% of Rs 40000, which is Rs 16000, and in 2024 they were 45% of Rs 60000, which is Rs 27000. The increase is Rs 27000 - Rs 16000 = Rs 11000. Either year's combined amount alone is not the increase, and the change in share alone does not give it either, because the total also changed.

items.question: The 2023 shares were Study 40%, Sleep 30%, Sports 10%, Entertainment 12%, Others 8%, on a total of Rs 40,000. The 2024 shares are shown in the pie chart, on a total of Rs 60,000. In the Monthly budget allocation pie charts, in 2024 the amount spent on Others is what percentage of the amount spent on Study in 2023?
items.explanation: The amount on Others in 2024 is 12% of Rs 60000, which is Rs 7200, and the amount on Study in 2023 is 40% of Rs 40000, which is Rs 16000. The ratio is 7200/16000 = 45%. A same-year ratio, a ratio of the shares, or the reciprocal all give wrong answers, because each amount must come from its own year's share and total.

items.question: The 2023 shares were Study 40%, Sleep 30%, Sports 10%, Entertainment 12%, Others 8%, on a total of Rs 40,000. The 2024 shares are shown in the pie chart, on a total of Rs 60,000. In the Monthly budget allocation pie charts, the amount spent on Study in 2024 is what percentage of the amount spent on Sleep in 2023?
items.explanation: Study in 2024 is 35% of Rs 60000, which is Rs 21000, and Sleep in 2023 is 30% of Rs 40000, which is Rs 12000. The ratio is 21000/12000 = 175%. Both amounts must be derived from their own year's share and total before the ratio can be formed, which is why same-year ratios are wrong.

items.question: What is the value of a? I. a squared - 7a + 12 = 0. II. a is greater than 3.
items.explanation: Statement I alone gives a = 3 or a = 4, since a squared - 7a + 12 factors as (a - 3)(a - 4) = 0, so it does not fix a. Statement II alone leaves a unbounded. Together, only a = 4 satisfies both, so both statements together are sufficient, but neither alone is sufficient.

items.question: Is the triangle right-angled? I. Two sides are 8 and 15 cm. II. The third side is 17 cm.
items.explanation: Neither statement alone gives all three sides. Together, 8 squared plus 15 squared is 289, which equals 17 squared, so by Pythagoras the triangle is right-angled. The verdict depends on the hidden fact of Pythagoras, not on either statement alone.

items.question: Is n divisible by 12? I. n is divisible by 3. II. n is divisible by 20.
items.explanation: Neither statement alone implies divisibility by 12. Together, since 3 and 20 are coprime, n is divisible by their product 60, which is a multiple of 12. The coprimality is the hidden fact that makes the two statements jointly sufficient.

items.question: Is x greater than y? I. x + y = 34. II. x - y = 12.
items.explanation: Statement I alone does not settle it: x = 24 and y = 10 satisfy x + y = 34 with x greater than y, while x = 10 and y = 24 also satisfy it with x less than y. Statement II alone gives x - y = 12, which is positive, so x is greater than y. So Statement II alone is sufficient. The two equations together would find x and y, but they are not needed to answer the question.

items.question: What is the speed of the stream? I. The boat speed in still water is 10 km/h. II. The downstream speed is 16 km/h.
items.explanation: Neither statement alone gives the stream speed. Together, the stream speed is downstream minus still-water speed, 16 - 10 = 6 km/h. Both statements together are needed, and neither alone is enough.

items.question: What is the HCF of two numbers? I. Their product is 720. II. Their LCM is 180 and one of the numbers is 36.
items.explanation: Statement I alone is not sufficient, since many pairs multiply to 720. Statement II alone is not sufficient either: the other number must divide 180 and have an LCM of 180 with 36, which allows 45, 90 and 180, giving HCFs of 9, 18 and 36. Together, the HCF equals product divided by LCM, which is 720/180 = 4.

items.question: What is the new average of 10 numbers after one number is replaced? I. The old average is 70. II. The number 50 is replaced by 90.
items.explanation: Neither statement alone gives the new average. Together, the total rises by 40, so the average rises by 40/10 = 4, giving 74. Both statements together are needed, and neither alone is enough.

items.question: What is the profit percentage on the article? I. The cost price is Rs 500. II. The marked price is Rs 800 and the discount is 25%.
items.explanation: Neither statement alone gives the profit. Together, the selling price is Rs 800 less 25%, which is Rs 600, so the profit is Rs 100 on Rs 500, which is 20%. Both statements together are needed, and neither alone is enough.

items.question: What is A's age? I. The ratio of the ages of A and B is 7:5. II. The sum of their ages is 72 years.
items.explanation: Neither statement alone gives A's age. Together, A is 7/12 of the total 72, which is 42 years. Both statements together are needed, and neither alone is enough.

items.question: Is a greater than 0? I. a squared is 36. II. a is not negative.
items.explanation: Statement I alone leaves a as 6 or -6. Statement II alone does not fix a value. Together, a is 6, which is greater than 0. Both together are needed. The other options claim a different statement is enough, which does not follow from the given facts.

items.question: In how many days can A alone complete the work? I. A and B together can complete it in 10 days. II. B alone can complete it in 15 days.
items.explanation: Neither statement alone gives A's time. Together, A does 1/10 - 1/15 = 5/150 of the work per day, so A alone takes 30 days. Both statements together are needed, and neither alone is enough.

items.question: What is the two-digit number? I. It leaves a remainder of 0 when divided by 7. II. It is a multiple of 9.
items.explanation: Neither statement alone fixes the number. Together, the two-digit multiples of 9 with remainder 0 on division by 7 leave only 63. The uniqueness comes from checking the whole range, which is the hidden step that makes the two statements jointly sufficient.

items.passage: In a survey, 300 employees attend training in Excel, Python and communication. 20% of them do only Excel, 30% do only Python and 15% do only communication. 30 do exactly Excel and Python, 20 do exactly Python and communication, 15 do exactly Excel and communication, and 40 do all three. Of those who do only Excel, one-half are female; of those who do only Python, one-third are female; of those who do only communication, two-thirds are female; of those who do exactly Excel and Python, one-third are female; of those who do exactly Python and communication, one-half are female; of those who do exactly Excel and communication, one-third are female; and of those who do all three, one-fourth are female.
items.question: The number who do only Excel is what percentage of the number who do exactly two activities?
items.explanation: Only Excel is 20% of 300, which is 60. The numbers doing exactly two activities are 30 + 20 + 15 = 65. So the required percentage is 60/65 = 1200/13%. The reciprocal ratio, the share of the total, or adding the all-three group to the numerator all give wrong answers.

items.question: How many of the 300 employees are female?
items.explanation: The female counts by region are 30, 30, 30, 10, 10, 5, 10, which add to 125. Each region's female count must be worked out from its own fraction before adding, because the fractions differ by region. The other options miss one region or use the male total instead.

items.question: The number of males who do all three (Excel, Python and communication) is what percentage of the total number of females?
items.explanation: There are 40 who do all three, of whom 10 are female, so 30 are male. The total number of females is 125, so the required percentage is 30/125 = 24%. Both the numerator and the denominator are themselves derived quantities, and using the all-three total or the grand total as the base gives the wrong options.

items.question: X is the sister of Y. Y is the father of Z. Z is the mother of W. How is X related to W?
items.explanation: Y is Z's father, so Y is W's grandfather. X is Y's sister, so X is the sister of W's grandfather, which is W's great-aunt. She is one generation further away than an aunt, and she is not W's grandmother.
items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Blood Relations

items.question: M is the daughter of N. N is the wife of O. O is the brother of P. How is M related to P?
items.explanation: N is M's mother and O, N's husband, is M's father. O is P's brother, so P is the sibling of M's father, which makes M P's niece. M is not P's daughter, sister or cousin.
items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Blood Relations
Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Blood Relations
items.question: A is the mother of B and C. C is the wife of D. D is the son of E. E is the brother of B. How is A related to D?
items.explanation: E is the brother of B, and A is the mother of B, so E is A's son. D is the son of E, so D is A's grandson, and A is D's grandmother. No other option describes this relationship.

items.question: M is the father of N and O. N is married to P. P is the mother of Q. O is unmarried. Which of the following is true?
options: O is the aunt of Q
P is the daughter of M
Q is the grandchild of M
Q is the nephew of O
items.explanation: N is married to P and P is the mother of Q, so Q is N's child. M is N's father, so Q is M's grandchild. O's gender is not given, so O may be Q's aunt or uncle; P is N's spouse, M's daughter-in-law, not M's daughter; and Q's gender is not given, so Q may be O's niece or nephew.
items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Blood Relations

items.question: In a certain code, each letter of a word is moved forward in the alphabet by its position in the word: the first letter by 1 place, the second by 2 places, and so on. For example, BANK is coded as CCQO. How is ROAD coded under the same rule?
items.explanation: Work out the rule from the example: in BANK, the first letter moves 1 place, the second 2 places, the third 3 places and the fourth 4 places, giving CCQO. Apply the same shifts to ROAD: R moves 1 place to S, O moves 2 places to Q, A moves 3 places to D and D moves 4 places to H, giving SQDH. The SQCE option comes from shifting vowels by 2 and consonants by 1, the reversed word comes from reversing without shifting, and the SQDG option differs from the correct code in the final letter only.
items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Coding Decoding

items.question: In a certain code, a word is first reversed. Then the first letter of the reversed word is moved 1 place forward, and each later letter is moved 2 places forward if the letter before it is a vowel, and 1 place back if the letter before it is a consonant. Two examples are given: COLD is coded as EKNE, and JUMP is coded as QLTL. How is SING coded under the same rule?
items.explanation: First find the rule from the examples: each coded letter depends on the letter before it, so the rule has to be worked out letter by letter rather than applied uniformly. For SING, reverse it to get GNIS. Then G moves 1 place forward to H; N moves 1 place back to M because the letter before it, G, is a consonant; I moves 1 place back to H because the letter before it, N, is a consonant; S moves 2 places forward to U because the letter before it, I, is a vowel, giving HMHU. The IPKU option reverses and shifts every letter by 2, the THPF option applies the chain without reversing, and the reversed word alone ignores the shifts.
items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Coding Decoding

items.question: In a code, a word is written as two numbers: the sum of the alphabet positions of its 1st and 3rd letters, followed by the sum of the positions of its 2nd and 4th letters. If BANK is coded as 1612, how is SING coded under the same rule?
items.explanation: For SING, the 1st and 3rd letters sum to 33 and the 2nd and 4th sum to 16, giving 3316. The total of all four positions, or the two sums in the wrong order, are the traps.
items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Coding Decoding

items.question: In a certain code, each letter of a word is shifted by the next letter in the word: a letter moves 2 places forward if the next letter is a vowel, and 1 place back if the next letter is a consonant. The last letter moves 1 place forward. Two examples are given: SPARE is coded as RRZTF, and TRAIN is coded as STCHO. Using the same code, the coded form BNQTE stands for which word?
items.explanation: Work out the rule from the examples: in SPARE, each letter's shift depends on the letter after it, so a letter before a vowel moves 2 places forward and a letter before a consonant moves 1 place back, with the last letter moving 1 place forward. Test the options against the code BNQTE: CLOUD gives BNQTE; CLOUT gives BNQTU; CLOWN gives BNNVO; PROUD gives OTQTE. Only CLOUD matches exactly, and each other option differs in exactly one coded letter, so the rule has to be applied to the whole word rather than guessed from a single letter.
items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Coding Decoding

items.question: What is the next number in the series: 5, 7, 9, 10, 13, 13, ?
items.explanation: The terms in odd positions rise by 4 and the terms in even positions rise by 3, so the next term, in an odd position, is the last odd term plus 4, which is 17. Continuing one step too far, or one step short, gives the other options.
items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Number Series

items.question: What is the next number in the series: 7, 11, 17, 25, 35, 47, ?
items.explanation: The differences between consecutive terms are 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, which themselves rise by 2 each time. The next difference is 14, so the next term is 47 + 14 = 61. Using a constant difference or the wrong step gives the other options.
items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Number Series

items.question: What is the next number in the series: 4, 8, 13, 26, 31, 62, ?
items.explanation: The series alternates between multiplying by 2 and adding 5. The next step is adding 5, giving 67. Applying the other operation, or applying both, gives the wrong options.
items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Number Series
Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Letter Series
items.question: What is the next term in the series: B, E, I, N, T, ?
items.explanation: The differences are 3, 4, 5 and 6, increasing by 1 each time, so the next difference is 7. T is the 20th letter, and 20 + 7 = 27, which wraps past Z to A, the 1st letter.

items.question: What is the next letter in the series: T, W, U, B, V, G, ?
items.explanation: The letters in odd positions advance by 1 places and those in even positions advance by 5 places, wrapping from Z back to A. The next term is in an odd position, so it is the last odd letter advanced by 1, which is W. Letters one step either side, or the result of the wrong progression, are the traps.
items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Letter Series

items.question: Statements: Some managers are leaders. All leaders are honest. No honest person is corrupt. Conclusions: I. Some managers are honest. II. No manager is corrupt. Which of the conclusions follow?
options: Both conclusions I and II follow
Neither conclusion I nor II follows
items.explanation: Some managers are leaders and all leaders are honest, so some managers are honest. Only some managers are leaders, so other managers could be corrupt, and the second conclusion does not follow. The other verdicts claim a conclusion that the premises do not support, or deny one that they do support.

items.question: Statements: All P are Q. No Q is R. Some S are P. Which of the following statements is definitely true?
items.explanation: Some S are P, and all P are Q, so some S are Q, which means some Q are S. That is the only statement that must hold: the S that are P are not R, but other S could be R, so 'No S is R' does not follow, and neither does 'Some S are R' or 'All S are Q'. The keyed statement in the earlier version made the mistake of turning some S into all S.

items.question: Statements: All books are novels. No novel is a poem. Conclusions: I. No book is a poem. II. Some novels are not poems. Which of the conclusions follow?
options: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow
items.explanation: All books are novels and no novel is a poem, so no book is a poem. Since no novel is a poem, some novels are certainly not poems, so both conclusions follow. The other verdicts claim a conclusion that the premises do not support, or deny one that they do support.

items.question: In a group of 180 students in a school, 35 do only Maths, 30 do only Science and 25 do only English. The number who do exactly two of the three is twice the number who do all three, and 42 do at least two of the three. How many do none of the three?
items.explanation: Let the number who do all three be x. Then exactly two is 2x, and at least two is 2x + x = 3x = 42, so x = 14 and exactly two is 28. Everyone is accounted for by only-one (35 + 30 + 25 = 90), exactly-two (28), all-three (14) and none, so none = 180 - 90 - 28 - 14 = 48. Using the exactly-two count, or the all-three count, or adding the all-three count to the answer, gives the other options.
items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Venn Diagram

items.question: Among the 120 students in a school, 25 do only Maths, 20 do only Science and 15 do only English, and 32 do none of the three. 8 students do all three of Maths, Science and English. How many do exactly two of Maths, Science and English?
items.explanation: The students doing only one subject number 25 + 20 + 15 = 60, and 32 do none, so those doing at least two number 120 - 60 - 32 = 28. Of these, 8 do all three, so those doing exactly two number 28 - 8 = 20. The at-least-two total 28 and the all-three count 8 are the traps.
items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Venn Diagram

items.question: Among the 120 students in a school, 25 do only Maths, 20 do only Science and 15 do only English. 20 students do exactly two of Maths, Science and English, and 8 do all three. How many do none of Maths, Science and English?
items.explanation: Those doing at least one subject number 25 + 20 + 15 + 20 + 8 = 88, so those doing none number 120 - 88 = 32. Forgetting the exactly-two group or the all-three group when adding up gives the wrong options.
items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Venn Diagram

items.passage: 7 people sit in a row from left to right. (1) G sits at the left end. (2) A sits immediately to the left of B. (3) C sits two places to the left of A. (4) E sits between C and A. (5) F sits immediately to the right of B. (6) D sits at the right end. Use the clues to work out the arrangement.
items.question: If F and D swap places, who sits immediately to the left of B?
items.explanation: Working out the arrangement from the clues: G is at the left end and D at the right end. C is two places left of A with E between them, so the order must be C, E, A, and A sits immediately left of B with F immediately right of B, giving G, C, E, A, B, F, D. Swapping F and D gives G, C, E, A, B, D, F. B is still in fifth place, and the person immediately to the left of B is A.
items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Seating Arrangement

items.question: Using the same arrangement, who sits between C and A?
items.explanation: In the solved order G, C, E, A, B, F, D, E sits between C and A. The answer needs the full arrangement, since no single clue places E between those two.
items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Seating Arrangement

items.question: In the arrangement of A, B, C, D, E, F and G, which of the following statements is definitely true?
options: G sits second from the left
D sits at the right end
A sits at the left end
items.explanation: In the solved order G, C, E, A, B, F, D, the statement 'D sits at the right end' holds, while each of the other statements contradicts the solved order. Only the complete solution settles this question.
items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Seating Arrangement

items.question: A hospital introduced a checklist for every surgery and surgical errors fell. The hospital claims the checklist caused the fall. Which of the following most strengthens the claim?
options: Errors also fell in another hospital.
No other change in staff, equipment or procedures happened in the same period.
items.explanation: If nothing else changed, the checklist is the most likely cause of the fall. The other options praise checklists or cite another hospital without ruling out alternative causes here.
items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Critical Reasoning

items.question: A school that starts classes later reports better exam results, so later starts improve results. Which of the following most weakens the claim?
options: Exams are held in the morning.
Students like sleeping late in the morning.
The school also hired better teachers and reduced class sizes in the same year.
items.explanation: Better teachers and smaller classes are rival explanations for the better results, so the later start may not be the cause. The other options do not offer any rival cause.
items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Critical Reasoning

items.question: A library extends its hours and membership rises. The library claims longer hours attracted members. The same month a new housing estate opened nearby, and the library also waived its joining fee. Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the library's claim?
options: Members said they liked the longer hours.
Membership also rose at a library that kept its old hours.
Longer hours cost the library more in electricity.
Branches that extended hours but kept the joining fee showed no rise, while branches that waived the fee rose whether or not hours changed.
items.explanation: The claim attributes the rise to longer hours, but the joining fee was waived at the same time, so the two changes are confounded. The fourth option separates them: where only hours changed, membership did not rise, and where only the fee changed, it did, so the rise tracks the fee waiver, not the hours. Members liking the hours says nothing about joining, a rise elsewhere could have a different cause, and the cost of longer hours is irrelevant to whether they caused the rise.
items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Critical Reasoning

items.question: A company that allows remote work has lower attrition than one that does not, even though pay is the same. What can be inferred?
options: Pay does not matter to employees at all.
Remote work is the only cause of low attrition.
All companies must allow remote work.
Remote work may contribute to lower attrition.
items.explanation: Attrition differs while pay is the same, which is consistent with remote work contributing to the difference. The other options turn a possible contribution into the only cause or a universal rule.
items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Critical Reasoning

items.question: Crime fell after more street lights were installed, so the lights reduced crime. What is the flaw in this reasoning?
options: Lights make streets brighter at night.
Street lights cost a lot of money.
Crime also fell in other towns.
Other changes, such as more police patrols in the same period, could explain the fall.
items.explanation: The argument assumes the lights were the only change, but patrols or other changes could explain the fall. The other options are facts about lights or crime that do not identify the reasoning error.

items.question: A man walks 8 km east and then 6 km north. He then turns and walks straight back towards his starting point, stopping halfway. How far is he from his starting point now, in km?
items.explanation: After the two legs he is 10 km from the start, the hypotenuse of a 8-6-10 triangle. Walking halfway back along the straight line leaves him 10/2 = 5 km away. The full distance, or half the sum of the legs, are the traps here.
items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Direction Sense

items.question: A and B start at the same point. A walks 6 km east, then 8 km north, then 6 km west. B walks 6 km south. How far apart are A and B, in km?
items.explanation: A ends 8 km north of the start, since the east and west legs cancel, and B ends 6 km south of the start, so they are 8 + 6 = 14 km apart. Either single distance alone, or a value that adds the cancelled legs, is wrong.
items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Direction Sense

items.question: Which of the following pairs shares the same relationship as Wheel : Car, where the first is the part of the second that makes contact with the surface or medium through which the second moves?
items.explanation: A wheel is the part of a car that touches the road, the surface the car moves over. A wing is the part of an aeroplane that meets the air, the medium it moves through. A road is the surface itself, not a part of the car. A driver operates the car but is not a part of it, and petrol is fuel that the car consumes, not a part that makes contact with the surface.

items.question: The International Monetary Fund was established in 1944. The World Bank was established in 1944. The World Trade Organization was established in 1995. Consider the following statements. (1) The International Monetary Fund was established before the World Trade Organization. (2) The World Bank and the International Monetary Fund were established in the same year. (3) All three institutions were established before 1950. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
items.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: 1944 comes before 1995. Statement 2 is correct: both were established in 1944. Statement 3 is incorrect: the World Trade Organization was established in 1995, after 1950.

items.question: A company has six departments with headcounts of 10, 25, 15, 30, 20 and 40. Consider the following statements. (1) The total headcount of the six departments is 140. (2) More than half of the departments have over 20 staff. (3) The largest department is four times the smallest department. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
items.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: 10 + 25 + 15 + 30 + 20 + 40 = 140. Statement 2 is incorrect: three departments, with 25, 30 and 40 staff, have over 20 staff, which is exactly half of six, not more than half. Statement 3 is correct: 40 is four times 10.
items.topic: Economic and Business Environment - Current Affairs

items.question: A government scheme has an outlay of Rs 900 crore: component A Rs 300 crore, component B Rs 270 crore, component C Rs 180 crore and component D Rs 150 crore. Consider the following statements. (1) Component A is one-third of the outlay. (2) Component B exceeds component C by Rs 100 crore. (3) Component D is less than one-fifth of the outlay. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
items.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: 300 out of 900 is one-third. Statement 2 is incorrect: 270 minus 180 is 90, not 100. Statement 3 is correct: 150 out of 900 is about 16.7 percent, which is less than one-fifth.

items.question: The minimum wage rises from Rs 300 per day to Rs 360 per day. Consider the following statements. (1) The daily wage rises by Rs 60. (2) The daily wage rises by 20 percent. (3) A worker who works 25 days a month gains Rs 1,500 a month. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
items.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: 360 minus 300 is 60. Statement 2 is correct: 60 out of 300 is 20 percent. Statement 3 is correct: 60 times 25 is 1,500.

items.question: Bank P has loans of Rs 5,000 crore with non-performing assets of 4 percent. Bank Q has loans of Rs 3,000 crore with non-performing assets of 5 percent. Consider the following statements. (1) Bank P's non-performing assets are higher in rupees than bank Q's. (2) Bank Q's non-performing asset rate is higher than bank P's. (3) Bank P's non-performing asset rate is higher than bank Q's. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
items.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: 4 percent of 5,000 is 200, while 5 percent of 3,000 is 150, so P's amount is higher. Statement 2 is correct: 5 percent is higher than 4 percent. Statement 3 is incorrect: it reverses the rates.

items.question: Inflation is a rise in the general price level. A price index rises from 120 to 126. Consider the following statements. (1) Inflation is 5 percent. (2) A basket that cost Rs 100 now costs Rs 105. (3) Prices fell. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
items.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: 6 out of 120 is 5 percent. Statement 2 is correct: a 5 percent rise turns Rs 100 into Rs 105. Statement 3 is incorrect: the index rose, so prices rose, not fell.

items.question: A bank's loan defaults rose from April. Three explanations are offered: a rate rise in February that applied to all borrowers, new lending rules introduced in January, and a drought in one region from March. Further facts: defaults rose only in the drought region, other regions were unchanged, and the rise began in April. Consider the following statements. (1) The rate rise is ruled out, because it applied to all borrowers but defaults rose in one region only. (2) The new lending rules are the most likely cause, because defaults rose after the rules were introduced. (3) The drought is supported as a cause, because the rise is concentrated in the drought region and began after the drought. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
items.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: a change affecting all borrowers cannot explain a rise confined to one region. Statement 2 is incorrect: the rules were introduced in January and applied everywhere, so timing alone does not support them, and the regional pattern contradicts them. Statement 3 is correct: the rise matches the drought in place and in timing.
items.topic: Economic and Business Environment - Current Affairs

items.question: A mutual fund must keep at least 65 percent of its money in equities to be called an equity fund. It holds Rs 65 crore of its Rs 100 crore in equities. Consider the following statements. (1) The fund holds exactly 65 percent in equities. (2) The fund qualifies as an equity fund. (3) The fund holds more than 65 percent in equities. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
items.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: 65 out of 100 is 65 percent. Statement 2 is correct: the rule requires at least 65 percent, and 65 percent meets it. Statement 3 is incorrect: 65 percent is not more than 65 percent.

items.question: A country's services exports were Rs 100 crore in 2021, Rs 150 crore in 2022, Rs 240 crore in 2023 and Rs 300 crore in 2024. Consider the following statements. (1) Services exports tripled from 2021 to 2024. (2) The fastest growth was in 2023. (3) Growth in 2024 was 25 percent. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
items.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: 300 is three times 100. Statement 2 is correct: growth was 50 percent in 2022, 60 percent in 2023 and 25 percent in 2024, so 2023 was the fastest. Statement 3 is correct: 300 minus 240 is 60, and 60 out of 240 is 25 percent.

items.question: Five states have gross domestic products of Rs 400 crore, Rs 350 crore, Rs 300 crore, Rs 250 crore and Rs 200 crore. Consider the following statements. (1) The state with Rs 350 crore is second in the ranking. (2) The largest state exceeds the smallest state by Rs 200 crore. (3) The states with Rs 300 crore and Rs 250 crore together are less than the largest state. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
items.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: 350 is the second largest of the five figures. Statement 2 is correct: 400 minus 200 is 200. Statement 3 is incorrect: 300 plus 250 is 550, which is more than 400, not less.
items.topic: Economic and Business Environment - Static GK

items.question: Demonetisation took place in 2016. The Goods and Services Tax was launched in 2017. The digital rupee pilot began in 2022. Consider the following statements. (1) Demonetisation came before the Goods and Services Tax. (2) The gap between the Goods and Services Tax and the digital rupee pilot is 5 years. (3) All three happened before 2020. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
items.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: 2016 comes before 2017. Statement 2 is correct: 2022 minus 2017 is 5. Statement 3 is incorrect: the digital rupee pilot began in 2022, after 2020.

items.question: A bank has branches in six cities: 12, 8, 20, 15, 10 and 5 branches. Consider the following statements. (1) The total number of branches is 70. (2) More than half of the cities have over 10 branches. (3) The city with the most branches has four times the branches of the city with the fewest. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
items.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: 12 + 8 + 20 + 15 + 10 + 5 = 70. Statement 2 is incorrect: three cities, with 12, 20 and 15 branches, have over 10 branches, which is exactly half of six, not more than half. Statement 3 is correct: 20 is four times 5.
